cues.en: No, thank you. So yeah, I titled this talk In Search of Tomorrow, and I wanted it to sort of evoke a journey, because we're going to go on a bit of a journey. So over the past, I guess, almost six years now, I have sort of been working on trying to find an answer to this question. What does programming look like in 10 years, right? And my first sort of real approach to this, my first actual
cues.zh: 不用，谢谢。我把这次演讲命名为《寻找明天》（In Search of Tomorrow），想唤起一种旅程的感觉，因为我们确实要踏上一段探索之旅。在过去大概近六年的时间里，我一直在努力寻找这个问题的答案：十年后的编程会是什么样？而我对此的第一次真正尝试，第一次实际——

cues.en: time that I was tasked with trying to figure this out a bit was, as Fernando said, at Microsoft. So I was a program manager on Visual Studio at Microsoft. And as time went on, I originally started as a program manager on the editor and eventually came to own the experience of using C Sharp and Visual Basic. And while I was there, I sort of carved out this little interesting position for myself, which is trying to figure out what Visual Studio will look like years from now.
cues.zh: 接到任务去搞清楚这个问题的经历，正如 Fernando 所说，是在微软。我当时在微软担任 Visual Studio 的项目经理。起初我是负责编辑器的项目经理，后来负责了 C# 和 Visual Basic 的整体使用体验。在那里的时候，我还为自己争取到了一个挺有意思的职责：去构想几年后的 Visual Studio 会是什么样子。

cues.en: What is the future of Visual Studio? If we were going to make this programming thing better, if we were going to make programmers more efficient, what would it look like? And in order to answer that question, I managed to convince my superiors to let me do a study. And so I did the, to my knowledge, only ever done end-to-end study of Visual Studio, where I sat behind a one-way mirror and watched people program and solve problems on a computer in this sort of very general set of tasks for a month and a half.
cues.zh: Visual Studio 的未来在哪？如果我们要让编程变得更好，让程序员效率更高，它会是什么样？为了回答这个问题，我说服了上司让我做一项调研。于是我开展了据我所知 Visual Studio 唯一一次端到端的调研，在一个半月里，我坐在单面透视镜后，观察大家在一系列常规任务中如何用电脑编程和解决问题。

cues.en: As a result of that, I gained a lot of insight into what it means to program, what it means to be a good programmer, and how we actually do it. This is important because as an industry, we're actually not very introspective. I loved it. We would have these guys who would come in, I only use the keyboard. I never ever touch the mouse.
cues.zh: 由此，我深入理解了什么是编程、怎样才算优秀的程序员，以及我们究竟是如何写代码的。这非常重要，因为我们这个行业其实很少自我审视。太有意思了，经常有人一进来说：“我只用键盘，绝不碰鼠标。”

cues.en: Well, we have videotape of them using the mouse about half the time, right? It turns out that depending upon what tasks you're doing, what your mental processes are kind of doing at a time, you have different modes of operating. And one of those modes typically is done with a mouse, not a keyboard. And so I did this study and started to design what I thought the future of programming would kind of look like.
cues.zh: 结果录像显示，他们大概一半时间都在用鼠标。事实证明，取决于你手头的任务以及当时的思维活动，你会有不同的操作模式，而其中一种模式通常用的是鼠标而非键盘。做完这项研究后，我便开始构想并设计我认为未来的编程应该是什么模样。

cues.en: It's specifically tool-oriented. That was what I was tasked with. I wasn't looking so much at the languages or any of that. There was somebody else's job that was. And so I built a bunch of interesting prototypes and stuff, and they've been slowly trickling out of Microsoft since then. But this is where I first started. I started at Microsoft on Visual Studio, imagining what programming will look like in 10 years, and I'm like, it will be really fast to write.
cues.zh: 它是纯工具导向的，因为那正是我的任务。我并没有过多关注编程语言本身，那是别人的工作。所以我做了一批很有意思的原型，自那之后它们也陆续从微软面世。但这就是我的起点：在微软的 Visual Studio 畅想十年后的编程，当时我的想法是：写代码会变得飞快。

cues.en: That's kind of where I got to, and it will not only be really fast, but you'll be able to navigate really efficiently. These were the two things that I latched onto. That study also taught me something very important. What that thing was led me to the next project, which was light table. What that study taught me was that
cues.zh: 差不多就是我当时想到的，它不仅会非常快，你还能非常高效地浏览。这是我抓住的两件事。那项研究还教给我一件非常重要的事。那件事引出了我的下一个项目，也就是 Lighttable。那项研究让我明白的是

cues.en: Despite, as Fernando said, Visual Studio is a monument to humanity. It is 55 million lines of code when I was there five years ago. It is a gigantic piece of software. But in that study, I found out that most of the things that are in Visual Studio weren't actually helpful. They could have been. They could have been useful. It wasn't that the features themselves weren't good, but they were dwarfed by the fact that everyone was playing computer inside of their head.
cues.zh: 尽管正如 Fernando 所说，Visual Studio 是人类的一座丰碑。五年前我在那儿时，它有 5500 万行代码。它是一个巨大的软件。但在那项研究中，我发现 Visual Studio 里大多数东西其实并不怎么有帮助。它们本可以。它们本可以很有用。并不是这些功能本身不好，而是每个人都在脑子里扮演计算机这件事让它们显得微不足道。

cues.en: This was how they came to understand the software that they were working with. This is how they came to understand programs they were unfamiliar with, even ones they were familiar with. When something goes wrong, your only action is read some code, imagine what the computer would do, and play it out in your head, write some stuff down, and just keep doing this over and over and over again, until eventually you have basically simulated the program and you found your error. The premise behind Lighttable was, what if we were directly connected?
cues.zh: 这就是他们理解自己正在使用的软件的方式。这就是他们理解不熟悉的程序的方式，甚至是熟悉的程序也如此。出错时，你唯一能做的就是读一些代码，想象计算机会做什么，在脑子里推演，写点东西下来，然后一遍又一遍重复，直到最终你基本模拟了整个程序，找到了错误。Lighttable 背后的前提是：如果我们直接连在一起会怎样？

cues.en: What if there was no time between change and result? What if we shortened the feedback loop to effectively nothing? And I think, you know, there were many interesting ideas, I think, in Lighttable, but the one that people really latched onto was what I called at the time the insta-repl. And the idea was you typed code on the left-hand side, and if there was anything that ran as a result of that, on the right-hand side, you'd see the code filled in with all the values.
cues.zh: 如果改变和结果之间没有延迟会怎样？如果我们把反馈循环缩短到几乎为零会怎样？我觉得，你知道，Lighttable 里有很多有趣的想法，但大家真正抓住的那个，是我当时称为 insta-repl 的东西。它的想法是：你在左边输入代码，如果有任何东西因此运行，右边就会看到代码被填上所有值。

cues.en: So if we zoom in on it, this is an enclosure, so it's a lispy syntax. But if I add 3 and 4, it shows me that the answer is 7. So I do some math. And then what's interesting is this defn thing is a function. And so the function takes two arguments. And you can see they got filled in as well. And you can see what the result is. And what this enabled was, as I typed, it did this. So I could literally watch the data flow through my program. There was no question.
cues.zh: 所以如果我们放大看，这是一个括号表达式，是 Lisp 风格的语法。但如果我把 3 和 4 相加，它会显示答案是 7。所以我做些数学运算。然后有趣的是，这个 defn 定义了一个函数。这个函数接收两个参数。你可以看到它们也被填上了值。你也能看到结果是什么。它带来的效果是，我一边输入，它一边就做这件事。于是我真的能看着数据在程序里流动。完全不用猜。

cues.en: what was going on. When I said that people were forced to play computer inside of their head, what they were trying to do was make the program observable, right? They were given this sort of opaque thing with a set of instructions explaining how it works. And the goal here was, let's just open the box and let you see inside of it. And that was really interesting, and it was useful. And there's lots of very neat things that came out of Lighttable.
cues.zh: 到底发生了什么。当我说人们被迫在脑子里扮演计算机时，他们想做的是让程序变得可观察，对吧？他们拿到的是某种不透明的东西，外加一套说明它如何工作的指令。而这里的目标是：我们干脆把盒子打开，让你看到里面。那真的很有意思，也很有用。Lighttable 里诞生了很多非常巧妙的东西。

cues.en: I mean it had other ideas too, you know, it had this sort of small talky notion of like I'm gonna put code like little snippets of code all over the place and embed running applications in it So that you know, I can sort of create my own Organizations for code, right? I'm not limited to just what I can put in a linear file. I can create this sort of Canvas upon which all this stuff sits. So we did light table and One of the things we we had sort of an explicit goal of
cues.zh: 我是说它还有别的想法，你知道，它有种 Smalltalk 式的小巧思：我可以把代码——一小段一小段的代码——放到各处，并在其中嵌入正在运行的应用。这样，你知道，我就能创建自己的代码组织方式，对吧？我不再局限于线性文件里能放什么。我可以创造一块画布，让所有这些内容都落在上面。于是我们做了 Lighttable，而我们的一个明确目标……

cues.en: was not just, unlike at Microsoft, where the goal was purely make programmers more efficient, our goal with Lighttable was actually, yeah, we want to make me more efficient. That's great and all. That has potentially huge economic value. But more importantly, we wanted to make programming more accessible. One of the things that we came to was this idea that the reason programming is so hard is because it's unobservable.
cues.zh: 并不只是——在 Microsoft，目标纯粹是让程序员更高效；而我们做 Lighttable 的目标其实是，对，我们想让我自己更高效。这很好，也有潜在巨大的经济价值。但更重要的是，我们想让编程更容易上手。我们逐渐意识到的一点是：编程之所以这么难，是因为它是不可观察的。

cues.en: because you can't see what's going on. You can't see the effects of change. You can't watch your data flow through. And so you're doing this replaying in your head. And Lighttable, with features like this, yeah, hey, we're pretty good for programmers, actually. That study that I did for Visual Studio, we replicated it with Lighttable to see what the difference was. And for a career programmer, hey, programming this way is about twice as fast.
cues.zh: 因为你没法看到正在发生什么。看不到改动的效果。也没法观察数据如何流过。于是你只能在脑子里反复推演。而 Lighttable 有这类功能，对，嘿，其实对程序员来说相当好用。我为 Visual Studio 做的那项研究，我们用 Lighttable 复现了一遍，看看差异在哪。对职业程序员来说，嘿，这样编程速度大约快一倍。

cues.en: And there were lots of interesting things that came out of that. For example, in Visual Studio, people would write large swaths of code before ever pressing the play button, basically. With this model...
cues.zh: 从中得出了很多有意思的东西。比如，在 Visual Studio 里，人们基本上会在按下运行按钮之前写一大段代码。而在这种模式下……

cues.en: people wrote little tiny bits and were trying it all the time. And as a result of that, they built up, as they were building up sort of abstractions and all these functions and this sort of set of primitives, they knew what every single one of them was doing. They knew it worked correctly. They knew what their result was going to be. And so that was great. Career programmer could be maybe twice as fast. Turns out that twice as fast actually isn't enough.
cues.zh: 人们只写很小的一点点，然后一直试。结果，他们在逐步构建抽象、各种函数和一组原语的过程中，清楚每一个东西在做什么。知道它能正确工作。知道结果会是什么。所以那很棒。职业程序员也许能快一倍。但事实证明，快一倍其实还不够。

cues.en: something that people have sort of a religious attachment to, right? These are our tools. These are the ways we express ourselves as programmers. And so 2x, while interesting and compelling, is not enough to get me to drop Emacs, right? Or is not enough to get me to get out of Visual Studio or whatever the case may be. So it didn't really get the sort of attention we had hoped for in that regard. Although, you know, we got tens of thousands of people using it. More importantly, though, it did nothing.
cues.zh: 这是人们有种宗教般执念的东西，对吧？这些是我们的工具。这些是我们作为程序员表达自己的方式。所以 2x 虽然有趣且有说服力，但不足以让我放弃 Emacs，对吧？也不足以让我离开 Visual Studio，或者别的什么。所以在这方面，它并没有真正得到我们期望的那种关注。尽管你知道，我们有几万人在用它。但更重要的是，它没有带来任何改变。

cues.en: for our other goal, this goal of making programming more accessible. And we tried to understand this. And that understanding resulted in an essay that I wrote a while back called Toward a Better Programming. And in it, I sort of realized that I had approached this problem. I used to say, I want to make programming better. And I realized I had made a classic rookie mistake, which to this room is probably
cues.zh: 至于我们的另一个目标，也就是让编程更容易上手。我们试着理解这件事。这种理解促成了我前阵子写的一篇文章，叫 Toward a Better Programming。在文章里，我多少意识到自己此前是怎么看这个问题的。我以前总说，我想让编程变得更好。后来我意识到自己犯了一个经典的新手错误，而对在座各位来说，这大概

cues.en: well-known and understood. I tried to answer a question I didn't really understand, right? Like, what is making programming better mean? What is better? That implies that there's something wrong. What is wrong with programming? What even is programming, right? It's kind of an interesting question to start to ask. And so we started doing some research. We asked a bunch of people, built a bunch of prototypes, tried to sort of develop an understanding for what we were actually trying to do.
cues.zh: 是众所周知、也能理解的。我试图回答一个自己其实并不真正理解的问题，对吧？比如，让编程变得更好到底是什么意思？什么叫更好？这暗示着有什么地方出了问题。编程到底哪里有问题？甚至，编程到底是什么，对吧？这其实是个挺有意思的起点问题。于是我们开始做了一些研究。我们问了一堆人，做了一堆原型，试着去理解我们到底想做什么。

cues.en: I sort of came to an answer about what is wrong with programming. If we're going to do anything to fix it, we have to have some notion of what it is we're actually fixing. And it came down to three properties. The first I basically already started to talk about is that programming is unobservable. I make some change in code unless I manage to execute that code path in manual clicking around on a screen or whatever. I have no idea what happened.
cues.zh: 我算是得出了一个关于编程哪里不对的答案。如果我们真想动手修好它，就得先知道我们到底在修什么。最后归结为三个特性。第一个我其实已经大致开始讲了，就是编程是不可观察的。我在代码里做了些改动，除非我手动在屏幕上点来点去、设法执行到那条代码路径，否则我根本不知道发生了什么。

cues.en: And as I'm making the changes, if I make a whole bunch of them, I have no idea what the effect of each individual change is, much less the effect of the entire aggregate of changes. And this is a lot of what we were trying to address with Lighttable, was trying to make programming more observable. But there's another problem, too. And that is that programming is indirect. So if I'm, let's do something fun. If I'm describing a drone, and I have this thing hovering over here next to me,
cues.zh: 而且在我做改动时，如果我一下子改了一大堆，我完全不知道每个单独改动有什么效果，更别说所有改动的整体效果了。这正是我们想用 Lighttable 解决的大部分问题：让编程变得更可观察。但还有另一个问题。那就是编程是间接的。所以如果我，来点好玩的。如果我在描述一架无人机，而这东西就在我旁边悬停着，

cues.en: If I want to make that drone do something using pick any language you want, I have to first translate it into that language. I have to first translate it into the computer. I have to think like the computer in order to get the computer to do what I want. This is very indirect mapping.
cues.zh: 如果我想让那架无人机做点什么，用任何你想用的语言，我都得先把它翻译成那门语言。我得先把它翻译进计算机里。我得像计算机一样思考，才能让计算机做我想做的事。这是非常间接的映射。

cues.en: If you look at the vast majority of errors that happen when people program, they come from relatively simple translation errors. It's this indirection that causes a lot of friction. When we were doing that study on Visual Studio, we saw this over and over again where somebody had the right solution.
cues.zh: 如果你看看人们编程时发生的绝大多数错误，它们都来自相对简单的翻译错误。正是这种间接性造成了很多摩擦。我们做 Visual Studio 那项研究时，一次又一次看到这种情况：某人其实有正确的解法。

cues.en: just along the way, they just did it slightly incorrectly. And again, it wasn't that their logic was incorrect or any of that. It's just literally the mechanical process of translating that logic into Python or C-sharp or whatever is not easy. We're not very good at it as human beings. And the last one, and this is something that career programmers really latch onto when I talk to them, is that programming is incidentally complex.
cues.zh: 只是过程中做得稍微不对。再说一遍，问题不在于他们的逻辑错了或者别的什么。而纯粹是把那套逻辑翻译成 Python 或 C-sharp 之类的机械过程并不容易。作为人类，我们并不擅长这件事。最后一个，也是职业程序员跟我聊天时特别会抓住的一点，就是编程具有偶然复杂性。

cues.en: What I mean by that is that the vast majority of what we do when we program has nothing to do with the problem we are trying to solve. A very, very simple demonstration of this is I like to pick on how long does it take to set up a dev machine from scratch. I watch people take the better part of a week doing this at Microsoft. That's just to get code to run. That's not even trying to do anything interesting yet. That's just to get started to start your problem.
cues.zh: 我的意思是，我们编程时做的绝大多数事情，跟真正要解决的问题毫无关系。一个非常非常简单的例子是，我喜欢拿“从零搭一台开发机要多久”来说事。我在 Microsoft 看到有人要花大半周才能搞定。这还只是让代码跑起来。甚至还谈不上做任何有意思的事。这只是为了能开始处理你的问题。

cues.en: And so when I say that programming is incidentally complex, I mean that we spend a great deal of time solving the problems around solving our problem. So to give you a simple example of this, this sort of demonstrate exactly how hard programming really is, right? We tried to come up, and we did this talk a while back where we went around and had a bunch of people try to build what we thought was one of the simplest possible programs you could imagine a normal person wanting to build.
cues.zh: 所以当我说编程有偶然复杂性时，我的意思是，我们花大量时间解决“围绕解决问题”的问题。举个简单例子，这正好说明编程到底有多难，对吧？我们试着提出一个例子，之前做过一次演讲，我们四处找人，让他们尝试构建一个我们认为普通人会想构建的最简单程序之一。

cues.en: which is a button on the screen that counts the number of times it's been clicked. And so I click the button. It says one, and two, and three, and that's it. If you think about this, like what it takes to build this little button, we'll assume you already understand HTML, which is a big jump. But we'll assume you know enough to write this little bit of HTML here. And then it's not so bad. It's just six lines of JavaScript. Well.
cues.zh: 就是一个屏幕上的按钮，能统计它被点击了多少次。于是我点按钮。它显示一、二、三，就这样。如果你想想，构建这个小按钮需要什么——我们先假设你已经懂 HTML，这已经是一大步了。再假设你足以写出这里这一小段 HTML。然后还没那么糟。只需要六行 JavaScript。嗯。

cues.en: Let's unpack exactly what's in the six lines of JavaScript. So first off, you have to understand the notion of identity, which is arguably one of the hardest problems in programming, even though it seems like it should be something very simple. I have to tell the computer, hey, that button that I just put on the screen, I'm still talking about that button. I want to work with that one.
cues.zh: 我们来拆解这六行 JavaScript 里到底有什么。首先，你得理解同一性的概念，这可以说是编程中最难的问题之一，尽管它看起来应该非常简单。我得告诉计算机：嘿，我刚放到屏幕上的那个按钮，我还在说那个按钮。我想操作的就是它。

cues.en: You then have to deal with scope, right? This, again, six lines of code has a function in it, which is creating a new scope, and things are weird in this sort of world. Things that you define in there don't escape, but if you talked about them above there, they're ambiguously escaping. You have the notion of mutable assignment. The vast majority of programming errors are the result of mutable assignment. You have closures, something that still most career programmers don't understand correctly. You have asynchrony, which is
cues.zh: 然后你得处理作用域，对吧？同样，这六行代码里有一个函数，它会创建新的作用域，而在这个世界里事情会很怪。你在里面定义的东西不会逸出，但如果你在上方提到它们，它们又会以模糊的方式逸出。你还有可变赋值的概念。绝大多数编程错误都是可变赋值造成的。你还有闭包，大多数职业程序员至今仍不能正确理解它。你还有异步，而它

cues.en: probably unquestionably the hardest problem in programming at this point. You have objects, and properties, and the DOM. That six lines of code contains the context of years of work. You have to have spent years to understand what all of those things are doing. Yeah, sure, somebody might be able to go to Stack Overflow, copy some of this out, and ta-da, I have a button that works. But that means they can't change it because they don't understand it.
cues.zh: 可能毫无疑问是当前编程中最难的问题。你还有对象、属性，以及 DOM。那六行代码背后是多年的工作积累。你得花好几年才能理解这些东西都在干什么。是啊，当然，有人也许能上 Stack Overflow，复制一些出来，然后——哒哒，我有个能用的按钮了。但这也意味着他们改不了它，因为他们并不理解它。

cues.en: Those six lines of code, you know, I joke here, like, too long didn't read for six lines. But that is kind of the reality, right? Programming is hard. The question is, does it have to be hard, right? Is this sort of intrinsic? My standpoint is no. But this is where we ended up with Lighttable, right? We had taken these...
cues.zh: 那六行代码，你知道，我在这儿开玩笑，六行代码还要“太长不看”。但这差不多就是现实，对吧？编程很难。问题是，它非得这么难吗？这是不是本质性的？我的立场是：不是。但这正是我们在 Lighttable 上走到的地方，对吧？我们把这些……

cues.en: This kind of language, we took JavaScript, we took Clojure, we took Python. We're like, well, if we remove the feedback loop, programming will be easy now, because you don't have to play computer in your head. But this didn't change. All of this is still true. All of this is still necessary. And so as a result of that, it didn't make things much better. And that's the fundamental problem with trying to make it more accessible, is programming is still programming, no matter how good of a tool you make for it.
cues.zh: 这类语言，我们拿了 JavaScript，拿了 Clojure，拿了 Python。我们想，好吧，如果去掉反馈循环，编程现在就会变简单，因为你不用在脑子里扮演计算机了。但这没有改变。所有这些仍然成立。所有这些仍然必要。所以结果就是，它并没有让事情好多少。而这就是试图让编程更易用时面临的根本问题：无论你把工具做得多好，编程仍然是编程。

cues.en: And the problem with that is that these languages and these tools were built around the idea that we were going to build applications, right? That the end result of programming is a little icon that you double click on your screen and does one thing and somebody writes it and they give it to you and that's that. But the reality is what we really want, when I started to think more about what it meant to make programming more accessible, it wasn't about making applications. We struggled with this for a long time, right? We're like, oh.
cues.zh: 问题在于，这些语言和工具都围绕一个想法构建：我们要做应用，对吧？编程的最终结果就是屏幕上一个小图标，你双击它，它做一件事，有人写好交给你，就这样。但现实是，当我开始更多思考“让编程更易用”意味着什么时，我们真正想要的并不是做应用。我们为此纠结了很久，对吧？我们想，哦。

cues.en: Well, it's going to be building websites, so we'll make it easy to build websites. But it's actually to do something far more fundamental. It's just a thing. Fundamentally, if you go back to the beginning of the 1970s, when a lot of what is modern computing came to be, the idea back then wasn't the single purpose appliances. The idea was a tool to think with.
cues.zh: 好吧，那会是建网站，所以我们就让建网站变简单。但它实际上是要做更根本的事情。它就是一件事。从根本上说，如果你回到 1970 年代初，现代计算的很多东西开始成形的时候，当时的概念并不是单一用途的设备。那个概念是一种用来思考的工具。

cues.en: And if we are going to make programming more accessible, ultimately what we are trying to do is make a thinking tool, not necessarily a tool for building large-scale applications, right? Because at the end of the day, the computer is the greatest thinking tool ever developed, right? If I know the magical incantation necessary to punch holes in this card, I can get the computer to think for me, right? And that is a hugely, hugely powerful thing.
cues.zh: 如果我们要让编程更易用，归根结底我们要做的是造一个思考工具，而不一定是构建大型应用的工具，对吧？因为说到底，计算机是有史以来最伟大的思考工具，对吧？如果我知道在这张卡片上打孔所需的神奇咒语，我就能让计算机替我思考，对吧？这是极其、极其强大的东西。

cues.en: When we went around pitching this to folks, we labeled it a superpower, because that is fundamentally what it is. It is one of the only times that given a computer, you can start with nothing else and create something of immense value, right? Just by knowing how to punch these holes. And so that's what sort of ultimately led us to this project that we're working on now. And that project's name is Eve. And it is this idea, okay, I started with,
cues.zh: 当我们到处向人们推介这个想法时，我们把它称为一种超能力，因为这从根本上就是它。这是极少数情况下，给你一台计算机，你可以从一无所有开始，创造出有巨大价值的东西，对吧？只要知道怎么打这些孔。所以这最终把我们引向了现在正在做的这个项目。这个项目叫 Eve。它就是这样一个想法，好，我从……开始。

cues.en: Visual Studio trying to make programmers better. Realized that the tools are actually not all the problem. It's like the model of programming itself is a problem. Got to Light Table like, hey, the feedback is now there. So that makes it observable. But it wasn't quite the way there. And it was still a tool. We were still approaching this from a tools perspective. Eve is, what would happen if we tried to solve this problem from the ground up?
cues.zh: Visual Studio，试图让程序员变得更好。后来意识到，工具其实并不全是问题。问题在于编程模型本身。到了 Light Table，心想，嘿，反馈现在有了。所以这让它变得可观察。但这还不完全对路。它仍然是一个工具。我们仍然是从工具的角度来接近这个问题。Eve 则是：如果我们从头开始解决这个问题，会发生什么？

cues.en: Ignoring basically everything that exists, what would you build if you could? If you could basically imagine building programming today, right? So the first approach of this, of course, as a programmer, was to take all of the things we thought were good about programming, and all of the sort of trends that were happening, like functional programming, immutability, and all of these things, we'll put them all in a pretty little package, and that's just going to work.
cues.zh: 如果抛开现有的一切，让你从零去构建，你会做什么？如果让你想象在今天去发明编程，对吧？作为程序员，最初的思路当然是，把我们认为编程中所有的好东西，以及当时流行的趋势，比如函数式编程、不可变性等等，全都打包在一起，觉得这样就肯定行得通。

cues.en: So the first prototype of this was a thing that I showed at Strange Loop, which is a software conference. It was a software conference that deals with a lot of the more interesting avant-garde ways of thinking about the world. And so the idea was, OK, we'll take functional programming and immutable data, and we will
cues.zh: 这个想法的第一个原型，是我在 Strange Loop 上展示的一个东西，那是一个软件技术大会。那个大会专门探讨很多关于世界的前卫有趣的思考方式。所以当时的思路是，好，我们把函数式编程和不可变数据拿过来，然后……

cues.en: put it in something that looks a lot like a Jupyter Notebook. And we'll make it so that you're literally working with the data. I right-click on a thing, and I tell it what I want to do with it. And you can see all the results. And don't get hung up, because it doesn't look super great at this point. I built this prototype in four days. But it was really interesting, because it took a problem that would normally take quite a long time.
cues.zh: ……放到一个很像 Jupyter Notebook 的东西里。让你能够直接直观地操作数据。比如我右键点击一个东西，告诉它我想怎么处理，就能立刻看到所有结果。先别太在意界面，因为它现在看起来不算很好看，这个原型是我花了四天做出来的。但这真的很有意思，因为它解决了一个平时要花相当长时间的问题。

cues.en: better part of a day, for example. So this was taking a bunch of data out of Mongo, doing, so usage data out of Mongo, and then doing some math on it, and then getting a graph out of it, right? And all of this, again, was done by just sort of like dragging and dropping and right-clicking on some things. And there are a bunch of interesting ideas in this. One is the idea that you're always kind of working with the domain itself. So you'll see here in a second, when I want to write out some math, I actually do it in
cues.zh: 比如大半天的时间。原本是从 Mongo 里导出一堆数据——也就是 Mongo 里的使用数据——做一些数学计算，然后生成一张图表，对吧？而所有这一切，只需要通过拖拽和右键点击就能完成。这里面有很多有趣的想法。其一就是，你始终是在直接与业务领域本身交互。待会儿大家就会看到，当我想写数学公式时，我实际上就是用……

cues.en: math, and by that I mean mathematical notation. Zoom ahead here, because I'm apparently being slow. All right, so I want to sum over all the x's and divide it by the number, and ta-da, I have average, yay. So the idea was, if you're working in a domain, let's say, for example, I have my drone example again. If I'm working with a drone, there's a drone on the screen. Instead of describing a set of operations that I'm performing, I just move the drone around, and it's capturing what those steps were.
cues.zh: ……数学记号来写。这里快进一下，因为我操作有点慢。好了，我想对所有的 x 求和再除以总数，搞定，平均值出来了，太棒了。所以核心想法是，如果你在一个领域里工作，举个例子，还是拿我的无人机来说。如果我是在操作无人机，屏幕上就会有一架无人机。我不需要用代码描述一系列操作，只需直接拖动无人机，它就会记录下这些步骤。

cues.en: And then I can parameterize them by data, or get a chart, or whatever I'm trying to do. So this was interesting. And we took a much better, much prettier, cleaned up version of this. We're like, this is awesome. We can build all sorts of things with it. Later in the video, I'll skip ahead. I show building a website this way, where you just have these tree of functions that do stuff. And it was interesting and cool. As a programmer, it was very exciting.
cues.zh: 然后我可以用数据对其进行参数化，或者生成图表，随便你想做什么。这真的很有趣。后来我们做了一个更好看、更完善、更整洁的版本。我们觉得这太棒了，可以用它来构建各种各样的东西。视频后面我会快进，展示用这种方式来建一个网站，全是由执行不同任务的函数树构成的。这非常酷，也很有趣。作为一个程序员，当时感到非常兴奋。

cues.en: And I happened to be at the opening of Brett Victor's laboratory, CDG, in San Francisco. And there were all of these non-programmers, brilliant, brilliant people, physicists, and mathematicians, and all these people there, don't know how to program. And we set, like I said, a much better version of this in front of them, and were like, try it. Right? We were like, we were excited. We were stoked. We're done. This is going to be amazing.
cues.zh: 我当时正好在旧金山参加了 Brett Victor 的实验室 CDG 的开幕式。现场有许多非程序员，非常非常聪明的人，物理学家、数学家，所有人都在那儿，但都不会编程。就像我说的，我们把一个体验好得多的版本摆在他们面前，说：试试看吧。对吧？我们当时特别兴奋，极其激动，觉得自己搞定了，这肯定会大放异彩。

cues.en: Actually, the reactions were really positive. People liked it. They thought it was really interesting. They got why they would want to use it. And then, much to our horror, we watched them not be able to do anything in it. And I will never forget the reactions we got, which was they were trying so hard. And they were very well-meaning. They genuinely wanted this to work. So they were willing to do things that most people probably would not really be willing to do.
cues.zh: 实际上，大家的反应非常积极。大家很喜欢，觉得特别有意思，也明白为什么要用它。但随后令我们惊恐的是，我们眼睁睁看着他们用它什么也做不出来。我永远忘不了当时的场景，他们真的尽全力在尝试。他们非常善意，真心希望这东西能成，所以愿意去做大部分人可能压根不愿尝试的事。

cues.en: But there was this thing that surprised me, this thing that they struggled with. Out of all the things that I expected to find out in this, the hardest thing for the non-programmers to work with was scope. So in functional programming, you end up with these deeply nested set of functions, right? Everything is about this magical tree of functions that you're gonna call. And the reactions that we got
cues.zh: 但有一件事让我非常惊讶，就是让他们苦苦挣扎的那个点。在我预想的所有问题中，非程序员最难理解和处理的竟然是作用域。在函数式编程中，最终会有这些层层深层嵌套的函数集合，对吧？一切都围绕着这棵你要调用的神奇函数树展开。而我们得到的反馈

cues.en: were really obviously bad. So like, somebody would look at it and go, you know, they had some data up at the top of the function stack and they had some calculation they wanted to do at the bottom of the stack, right? And they're like, I want this down here. And you're like, kind of look at it, I mean, well, you can't, I mean, you'd have to pass that through all of these and you can't really do that. And they're like, I don't understand, I see it, it's right there, why can't I use it here, right? Okay, fine, if I can't do that, can I use this up there?
cues.zh: 显然非常糟糕。比如有人看着它会说——他们有些数据在函数栈的顶层，而想做的计算却在栈底，对吧？他们就会说：“我想把这个数据拿到下面来用。”你看了看就会说：“额，不行啊，你必须把它一路传过所有这些层级，实际上你没法直接用。”他们就会说：“我不理解，我明明看得到，它就在那儿，为什么我不能在这儿用呢？”行吧，如果不能这样，那能把下面的这个放到上面去用吗？

cues.en: No, you can't really do that either. We would have to thread it through going back up. It was like this really, I no longer believed the arguments I was making. Because you're trying to understand, well, scope is really important. You need it for functions, and functions are really important. And I don't know. That's something we can't do. And so we try to do a bunch of things. We try to make this nicer. We're like, OK, well, we'll make it look prettier.
cues.zh: 不行，那也不行。我们得把它一路往上层层传递回去。这真的很让人崩溃，我自己都开始怀疑自己说的这套道理了。因为你在努力解释说，作用域很重要，函数需要它，而函数又非常重要。但我也不知道了。反正就是做不到。于是我们尝试了各种办法，想把体验做顺畅一点。我们想，好吧，那至少把它做得更美观一些。

cues.en: And we tried to do a bunch of things to make the scoping thing less of an issue. So there was no variable shadowing. We had a much simpler version of scope. We drew arrows. We colored things the same. We tried to do all of these different things. Nothing worked. It seemed like it was kind of like just this fundamental problem that was really hard to get over. And so that led us down this very odd line of questioning, which is, well, if
cues.zh: 我们试了各种办法来减少作用域带来的困扰。比如去掉了变量遮蔽，采用了极度简化的作用域机制。我们画了箭头，把相关元素涂成相同颜色，尝试了各种各样的方法。但全都没用。这似乎就是一个极难逾越的根本性难题。于是这把我们引向了一个非常奇特的思考方向，那就是：如果……

cues.en: Our first attempt at this, what the industry seems to think the future of programming is, is, like I said, functional and immutable and yay. If that's not right, and scope is kind of a problem, which basically encompasses all of programming, where do we go from here, right? Like, what does it mean to remove scope from programming? So if you think about it, without scope, you can't have functions, so that's already scary to begin with. It also is that,
cues.zh: 我们的第一次尝试，也就是业界普遍认为的编程未来——正如我说的，函数式、不可变等等，一片叫好。如果这条路不对，而几乎贯穿了整个编程的作用域又是个大难题，那我们接下来该何去何从？比如，从编程中彻底移除作用域意味着什么？你想想看，没有作用域就无法拥有函数，这光是想想就已经够吓人了。而且还不止于此，

cues.en: When you're building up these nested data structures that you have, they're creating scopes. You're starting to worry a lot about where something is in this tree of data. And you don't want to duplicate, because you've put that data somewhere, and you put it in another place, then they're going to be out of sync, and you have all these problems. So it's another version of the scoping problem. So you can't have functions. You can't really have data structures. If you don't have data structures, you don't have anything that can keep things in order anymore. So you don't have ordering.
cues.zh: 当你构建这些嵌套的数据结构时，它们也在创建作用域。你开始格外操心某个数据位于数据树的哪个位置。而且你不想重复存，因为一旦把数据放一处又放另一处，它们就会失去同步，冒出各种问题。所以这是作用域问题的另一种形式。这么一来，你既不能有函数，也不能真正拥有数据结构。而如果没有数据结构，你也就没有任何东西来维持顺序了。所以你连顺序也无法保留。

cues.en: So if you think about what programming is, if you asked a career programmer what programming is, they would probably say an ordered set of steps, typically executing functions over a set of data. All of that falls away if you remove scoping. And so we started to look into, well, has anything ever worked this way? And there is at least one massively successful example that works exactly like this. And that is Excel.
cues.zh: 如果你思考一下什么是编程，去问一个职业程序员，他们大概会说，编程就是一组有序的步骤，通常是在一组数据上执行函数。但如果你去掉了作用域，这一切就不复存在了。于是我们开始琢磨，以前有东西是这么运作的吗？还真有，至少有一个极其成功的例子就是这么干的。那就是 Excel。

cues.en: So Excel has a single data structure, but you don't work with the data structure directly. It has no scoping. If I can see a value, I can use it anywhere. It has no inherent ordering. It has scalar functions, but you're not nesting these deeply. You're writing out basically the equivalent of a mathematical formula, and it never goes deeper than that. So it has all these properties, and that is a fantastic result, and also a terrible result, but a fantastic result first. It is a fantastic result.
cues.zh: Excel 只有一种数据结构，但你并不直接操作它。它没有作用域。只要我能看到某个值，就能在任何地方使用它。它没有固有的顺序。它有标量函数，但你不会深度嵌套它们。你基本上就是在写类似于数学公式的东西，仅此而已。所以它具备所有这些特性，这既是个了不起的结果，也是个糟糕的结果，但首先它非常了不起。确实很了不起，

cues.en: because 800 million people use Excel every single day. It is unquestionably the most accessible thinking tool available to us. And people have done amazing, truly amazing things with Excel. I was telling this story at lunch that I had this opportunity to talk with some folks at a Fortune 500 company, right, in this cruise line. And they have this spreadsheet. There was 10 gigs in size.
cues.zh: 因为每天有 8 亿人在使用 Excel。它毫无疑问是我们能接触到的门槛最低的思考工具。人们用 Excel 创造过惊人的、真正不可思议的奇迹。我午饭时还聊起这事，我有机会跟一家世界 500 强邮轮公司的人聊过。他们有一个表格，足足有 10 GB 大小。

cues.en: It had been built up over a decade. No professional programmer had ever touched this spreadsheet, but it modeled the entirety of a Fortune 500 company's business. They could have nuked every other system and run it off of this spreadsheet. This is amazing. Totally utterly amazing. And so that's great. Now, at the same time,
cues.zh: 这个表格花十年时间一点点搭建起来。没有任何专业程序员碰过它，但它却建模了一家世界 500 强企业的全部业务。他们就算干掉所有其他系统，只靠这个表格也能运转。这太不可思议了。简直绝了。这固然很好，但与此同时，

cues.en: This is the downside. Excel wasn't meant to do that kind of thing. So they would joke around. They're like, yeah, if we made any changes to the spreadsheet, we had to go to lunch. Because it took an hour and a half for it to propagate. And Excel is constrained. It is a two-dimensional grid of numbers. If your problem is not easily specified as a two-dimensional grid of numbers, kind of out of luck. So we looked a little bit more. And we found that there was one other case that worked this way. Again, massively successful.
cues.zh: 弊端也随之而来。Excel 本来就不是用来干这种事的。所以他们经常开玩笑说，每次改完表格，大家就得去吃个午饭。因为要花一个半小时数据才能全部更新完。而且 Excel 有其局限性，它是一个二维数字网格。如果你的问题很难用二维数字网格来描述，那就没辙了。于是我们进一步探寻，发现还有另一个案例也是这种运作方式，同样极其成功。

cues.en: And that is relational databases. Relational databases have the same set of properties. If you can see a value, you can use it anywhere. If you can see a table, you can use it. Barring access rules, basically. There's no inherent ordering either to the code, the execution, any of it. Even the data has no inherent ordering. You order it as you will. And again, no deeply nested functions or any of this crazy scope stuff going on. You just have basically
cues.zh: 那就是关系型数据库。关系型数据库具备同样的一套特性。只要你能看到某个值，就能在任何地方使用。只要你能看到某张表，就能直接用，除去权限规则基本都是这样。无论是代码还是执行过程，都没有任何固有的顺序。甚至数据本身也没有固有顺序，想怎么排就怎么排。同样，也没有深度嵌套的函数，或者乱七八糟的作用域机制。基本上就只有

cues.en: functions and scalar values. And that is a great result, again, certainly not accessible like Excel, but it solves the other side of the equation. It is a flexible thing. The world runs on relational databases. At the end of the day, basically every bit of data ends up in one of them. And we have built games and websites, all the things you couldn't imagine really building in Excel. So we discovered this, like, hey, relational databases is an interesting case.
cues.zh: 函数和标量值。这同样是个很棒的结果。虽然它肯定不像 Excel 那样容易上手，但它解决了问题的另一面。它非常灵活。整个世界都运行在关系型数据库之上。说到底，基本上所有数据最终都会落入其中。我们用它构建了游戏、网站，各种你无法想象真正能用 Excel 做出来的东西。所以我们发现，嘿，关系型数据库是个很有意思的案例。

cues.en: see what people have been saying about them recently. There's got to be stuff other than Postgres out there that we can look into. And that's where we ended up on research out of here, actually. Joe Hellerstein's lab, the Boom Lab, had been working on a language called Bloom. And they were working on that language to do distributed systems. The idea behind it was that it was a query language, so a little bit like SQL, but it was based on data log. If you know what prologue is, it's kind of like prologue's little cousin.
cues.zh: 看看大家最近都在讨论些什么。除了 Postgres 肯定还有别的东西值得研究。实际上，我们就是顺着这个方向找到了这儿的研究成果。Joe Hellerstein 的实验室，也就是 Boom Lab，一直在研发一种叫 Bloom 的语言。他们做这门语言是为了构建分布式系统。其背后的理念是将其作为一种查询语言，有点像 SQL，但它是基于 Datalog 的。如果你了解 Prolog，它有点像 Prolog 的表弟。

cues.en: does a lot less and is a lot simpler and is able to be a lot faster as a result. And they were building distributed systems. So they re-implemented Hadoop. And we were like, oh, that's really amazing because it was orders of magnitude smaller and all these great things. Could we build a website this way? Could we take this, maybe stretch it a little bit, think about it in a slightly different way, and how far could we take it? So I built this prototype. This is ultimately actually the prototype we raise money on.
cues.zh: 功能少得多，也简单得多，因此速度快上不少。而且他们当时在做分布式系统，甚至重新实现了 Hadoop。我们当时就想，哇，这也太神了，因为代码量小了几个数量级，还有各种优势。那我们能用这种方式做网站吗？我们能不能借鉴一下，稍作拓展，换个思路，看看究竟能走多远？于是我做了这个原型。实际上，我们最终就是凭这个原型融到了资。

cues.en: It's a very interesting thing, because if you read what these little things do, we had an intuition, which is that Prolog, or Datalog, or any of these, is written in predicate logic. Predicate logic is pretty hard to get your head around, but if you think about it, it kind of looks like fill-in-the-blank sentences, like those mad lib books we had when we were kids. It's like, put a color here.
cues.zh: 这非常有趣，因为仔细看看这些微小逻辑的作用，我们当时有个直觉：Prolog、Datalog 这类语言都是基于谓词逻辑编写的。谓词逻辑挺难理解的，但琢磨一下就会发现，它其实就像填空造句，类似我们小时候玩的那种填词游戏书。就像是，“在这里填一种颜色”。

cues.en: And if you squint, and you think of it that way, if you think of these predicates that way, and you think of horn clauses as like, when you see this thing, do this thing, you get this kind of very natural way of thinking about it. So this is the incrementer button, right? That little button I was talking about before, say like, well, when I'm setting defaults, remember that the counter is zero. And when the counter has a value, draw this button. And when that button is clicked, change the counter as whatever its current value is to the value plus one, right?
cues.zh: 如果你退一步从这个角度去看，这样去理解这些谓词，把 Horn 子句看作“只要出现这种情况，就执行这个操作”，就会产生一种非常自然的思考方式。比如这就是那个自增按钮，对吧？就是我之前提到的那个小按钮，逻辑就像是：在设置默认值时，记住计数器为 0；当计数器有值时，绘制这个按钮；而当点击这个按钮时，把计数器的当前值加 1，对吧？

cues.en: And so like I said, we built interesting things out of it. We always build to do MVC, because that's what everyone builds. But started building interesting things out of it. And we started to realize this crazy way of programming that has no data structures, has no inherent ordering. When I built this prototype originally, it didn't even have aggregation, which is interesting. Sort of made us realize that a lot of the things we think are fundamentally necessary for programming just aren't. You don't need them at all, actually.
cues.zh: 正如我所说，我们用它做出了些很有意思的东西。我们照例先做了个 TodoMVC，因为大家都会做这个。但接着我们开始做更有趣的玩意儿。并且我们开始意识到，这种没有数据结构、没有固有顺序的编程方式简直不可思议。我最初做这个原型时，它甚至都没有聚合操作，这挺有意思的。它让我们明白，很多我们以为编程必不可少的基础特性，其实根本不需要。实际上你完全用不着它们。

cues.en: And sort of as an interesting example of this, not only, yeah, we built this website and you could say, oh, well, that's a toy or whatever. The IDE that it was written in was written in it. And I know a thing or two about building IDEs at this point. I've built a few. You know, Visual Studio is 55 million lines of code. Lighttable, which does far less than Visual Studio and was designed specifically to be as small as humanly possible, was over 10,000 lines of code. This was 600.
cues.zh: 作为一个有趣的例子，不只是这样——是啊，我们做了这个网站，你可能会说，哦，那是个玩具之类的。但写它用的 IDE 就是用这门语言写的。说到做 IDE，我现在也算略知一二。我做过几个。你知道，Visual Studio 有 5500 万行代码。Lighttable 做的功能比 Visual Studio 少得多，还专门设计得尽可能小，也有 1 万多行代码。而这个只有 600 行。

cues.en: But we're talking about a totally different way of thinking about the world. Not only was it 600 lines, it was written in a week in a language that had no tools, that didn't even have aggregation, right? Like it had bugs in it, and we still managed to write this in a week. And so that is a tremendously awesome result, that we can take some of the things that Joe's group had learned about distributed systems and apply them more generally to these other places. And if you squint at this,
cues.zh: 但我们谈论的是一种完全不同的看待世界的方式。它不仅只有 600 行，还是在一周内用一门没有工具、甚至连聚合都没有的语言写出来的，对吧？它还有 bug，我们仍然在一周内把它写出来了。所以这是个极其了不起的结果：我们可以把 Joe 的团队在分布式系统上学到的一些东西，更普遍地应用到这些其他领域。而如果你眯着眼看这个，

cues.en: it starts to kind of look like one of the holy grails of programming, right? It kind of starts to look like an executable, an English executable specification, right? I read it to you, and if you think about the description you would give of the incrementer button, it's not very far from this, except maybe the when setting defaults part of it, right? And that's obviously pretty surprising and like really interesting, right? Again, this is one of those things we've wanted for forever, but we found out
cues.zh: 它开始有点像编程界的圣杯之一，对吧？它开始看起来像一份可执行的、英文的可执行规格说明，对吧？我读给你听，如果你想想你会如何描述那个递增按钮，其实和这个差不太远，也许除了其中 when setting defaults 那部分，对吧？这显然相当令人惊讶，也非常有意思，对吧？再说一次，这是我们一直想要的东西之一，但我们发现

cues.en: that actually this way of programming isn't that great. A lot of people still think that the English specification is the future of programming. If we ever get there, we've made it, and we're kind of done. And I no longer believe that's true. The reason why, after having programmed this way for a little while, is that if you read an English specification, every line of that English
cues.zh: 其实这种编程方式没那么好。很多人仍然认为英文规格说明就是编程的未来。如果我们真能做到那一步，我们就成功了，差不多就大功告成了。而我不再相信这是真的。原因在于，用这种方式编程一段时间后，我发现：当你读一份英文规格说明时，其中的每一行英文

cues.en: requires you having understood and internalized every previous line that was written. If you think about a big part of what makes programming hard, or a big part of dealing with complex systems, is being able to box parts of them up. Like, I don't need to know about this, I don't need to know about this, I can just go with this.
cues.zh: 都要求你已经理解并内化了之前写下的每一行。想想编程之所以难，或者处理复杂系统之所以难，很大一部分原因在于能否把其中一些部分封装起来。比如，我不需要了解这个，我不需要了解这个，我只要用这个就行。

cues.en: And these English specifications required you to basically understand the whole thing all the time. And yeah, they were shorter, so maybe you could reasonably do that. But when we actually tested this out with people and sat them in front of it, they were like, I can read these programs. I get what they're doing. No one was successful in writing one, right?
cues.zh: 而这些英文规格说明要求你基本上始终理解整体。是的，它们更短，所以也许你还能合理地做到这一点。但当我们真的拿它来给人测试，让他们坐在它面前时，他们会说，我能读懂这些程序。我明白它们在做什么。可没有人成功写出过一份，对吧？

cues.en: which is kind of interesting. And yeah, you could argue maybe it was our tooling, maybe it was our strategy, maybe it was whatever. But I think it's probably actually more fundamental than that. Like I said, I think it has to do with this context problem, that every line requires the context of all the previous lines. And so we get, OK, let's try something totally different. We know this Excel thing works. Could we make it look like Excel? And so we started to realize that these operations
cues.zh: 这还挺有意思的。是的，你可以说是我们的工具问题，可以说是策略问题，或者随便什么问题。但我觉得实际上比这更根本。就像我说的，我认为这跟上下文问题有关，每一行代码都需要前面所有行的上下文。所以我们就想，好，咱们试试完全不同的东西。我们知道 Excel 那一套行得通。能把它做成类似 Excel 的样子吗？于是我们开始意识到这些操作

cues.zh: 可以在表格上可视化地执行，因为本质上这里就只有这些东西。在这个例子里，可能有点看不清，先不用太在意。但我做的是，这是 Eve 第一次与外界交互。它给我们发了一条短信。我们的做法是，底部有这一排按钮，你们可能看不清，但上面写着我们的名字。如果你点了其中一个按钮，就会给那个人发短信。它的运作方式是，系统内部有一些表格，

cues.en: that had event information in them, and had the people in them, and then we would join those two things together. And now you can see every time I click on one of these, it has the information for Chris, or Jamie, or Rob, and has a fake version of our phone numbers. But we actually did do this with our real phone numbers at one point. And so it's kind of like writing this thing in Excel, again, with some more interesting abilities than Excel usually has. We can join things. It had basically the properties of a relational database.
cues.zh: 里面包含了事件信息和人员信息，然后我们把这两者做 join 连接。现在你可以看到，每次我点击其中一个，就会显示 Chris、Jamie 或 Rob 的信息，还有一组虚构的电话号码。但我们之前确实用真实号码跑过。所以这有点像在 Excel 里做这件事，而且具备一些比普通 Excel 更有趣的能力。我们可以做 join。它基本上具备了关系型数据库的特性。

cues.en: And this was neat. It worked, for some definition of worked. It allowed you to do relatively simple things, but we found a bunch of problems with it. You just have these values, they just have kind of like random names. But it did kind of prove to us that you could start
cues.zh: 这很棒。它跑通了，某种意义上算成功了。它能让你做相对简单的事情，但我们发现了一堆问题。首先，一旦你建好了这个漂亮的小表格，你就丢失了所有关于这些信息来源的上下文。而在做开发时，这其实是非常关键的信息。你眼前只有这些值，名字也起得有些随意。但这确实向我们证明了，也许可以开始

cues.en: maybe treating this as a very different problem. Maybe instead of thinking about writing code, even if it were English code, maybe you could think of it as operations on these tables, and you could do it very visually, and you could do it almost essentially just mouse-driven, and it could look like Excel. We sort of ran into a bunch of roadblocks here, like I said.
cues.zh: 把它当作一个完全不同的问题来对待。也许不用总想着写代码——哪怕是英语自然语言代码——而是把它看作对这些表格的操作，非常直观、几乎完全靠鼠标驱动，而且长得像 Excel。不过就像我说的，我们在这里遇到了一堆拦路虎。

cues.en: Just like a very simple example of this is not knowing where anything came from, but as you started building up these more complex tables, you realize that people don't really think of the data this way. They're like, they have to think about keys a lot, right? And like joining on the keys and it was still pretty hard. It wasn't the right solution. And it was shortly after this one that were like, well guys, I don't know yet about how to do the whole like make this thing accessible, but can we at least
cues.zh: 最简单的例子就是不知道东西来自哪里，但当你开始构建更复杂的表时，就会发现人们并不是这样思考数据的。他们得频繁去考虑键（key），对吧？还要考虑基于键做 join，这依然很难。这不是正确的解法。就在这之后不久，我们想，好吧大家，我还不知道具体怎么把门槛降下来，但我们至少能不能

cues.en: prove that it's a good idea, that the foundation of this is a good idea. Because we had essentially broken this problem up into several problems. The first was, could we find a version of programming that was very simple? And by that, I mean of few parts. And that version of programming has to be something that I could use, as well as it's going to work on Excel-like problems, too. So it had to be a general purpose language. But it needed to be very simple. And so we really, really liked
cues.zh: 证明这是个好主意，证明它的底层基础是个好主意。因为我们本质上已经把这个问题拆成了几个问题。第一个是，我们能不能找到一种极简的编程范式？所谓极简，是指由极少的构件组成。而且这种编程范式既要我能用，又得能处理类似 Excel 的问题。所以它必须是通用语言，但也必须足够简单。因此我们非常非常喜欢

cues.en: the stuff out of the Boom Lab, and we had built some interesting things, but we wanted to deal with it more. We wanted to really try and develop some stuff with it and see what happened. And then we draw our clock, and this is just me being bad at math. And then they had this little language down here that allowed you to describe UI. That one, again, suffered from the same problems that I described before, which was that you lost all the context when you're building up these tables, and it didn't really fit the model very well.
cues.zh: 所以，一个即使专业程序员清楚该怎么做也随随便便要花 30 分钟的问题（要是不清楚，天知道要花多久），现在 30 秒就能搞定，对吧？只要换一种思路看待问题，我们的效率其实能高得多。不过，这个版本同样存在我前面提到的那些问题：在构建这些表的过程中会丢失所有上下文，而且它其实不太契合这个模型。

cues.en: So we tried this other thing. We're like, hey, the UI builder thing worked out pretty well. Let's clone Foursquare. Let's clone a production-ready website and see what that looks like. And each time we build a new Eve to try and do this, to try and understand it, and we test it with people. This one was good enough to build a production-ready clone of Foursquare. It was abysmal doing it. It was really, really bad, although not because of the UI editor. That worked out really well.
cues.zh: 于是我们又试了别的方法。我们想，既然 UI 构建器效果挺不错，不如来克隆一个 Foursquare 吧，克隆一个生产级的网站看看效果。每次我们都会构建一个新版本的 Eve 来尝试和探索，并找人测试。这个版本确实强大到能克隆出一个生产级的 Foursquare。但开发过程简直糟透了，真的非常非常难受，虽然这并不是 UI 编辑器的问题，UI 编辑器本身很好用。

cues.en: But the way we wrote queries in this was really awkward. We tried to mix the two. So we had the tables, and then we had the information, basically the sources of all the information from the tables up at the top, and it kind of looked like a SQL-y looking language. It was just bad. It's hard to explain exactly what was so bad about it until you use it and you fully realize exactly how bad it is. I don't have enough time to show it, and I don't...
cues.zh: 但在这个版本里写查询的方式特别别扭。我们试图把两者融合起来：我们有表，顶部还有这些表的所有信息源，看起来有点像类 SQL 语言。简直太烂了。除非你亲自用过，彻底体会到它有多反人类，否则很难解释清楚到底有多烂。我时间不够就不展示了，而且我也……

cues.en: I want to be ashamed, so I'm going to skip that one. But it was still interesting. It was the first time we did not have to write any code to build a real website. You could do this purely without typing anything, which was interesting, again. But it still wasn't right. So the next step after this was what we initially released. So we're all open source. And this is what we pushed out when we open sourced.
cues.zh: 我可不想公开处刑，所以就跳过那段了。不过它依然很有意思。这是我们第一次一行代码都不用写就建出了一个真实的网站。你完全不用键盘输入任何内容就能做出来，这确实很有趣。但它依然不够对味。所以这之后的下一步，就是我们最初发布的版本。我们是全开源的，而这就是我们开源时推出的版本。

cues.en: And it was based on this intuition that, well, all of our attempts of writing queries not in a query language that a programmer would understand have kind of been crappy. But we had this intuition that when we passed around queries to each other, we drew them on the board. And we drew them as what looked like entity relationship diagrams, if you know what those are, little bubbles with lines between them. And we realized, well, if we draw them that way to explain them to each other, could we make them work?
cues.zh: 它的灵感源于一种直觉：我们之前所有“不用程序员理解的查询语言来写查询”的尝试，全都挺烂的。但我们有一种直觉，那就是每次互相交流查询逻辑时，我们都是在白板上画出来的。画出来的样子很像实体关系图（如果你知道那是啥的话），就是几个带连线的小气泡。于是我们意识到：既然我们互相解释时是这么画的，那能不能直接让这种形式跑起来呢？

cues.en: And we hesitated going in this direction because we know lots of problems with this kind of visual programming. And we had even built the boxes and arrows version of this long early in our process and realized this is not going to work. But this is a very different property because what you're describing is not a set of steps or a data flow. You're describing a shape. You're saying, I am looking in the database for a shape. And specifically, this is a famous shape.
cues.zh: 我们当时犹豫要不要走这个方向，因为我们深知这种可视化编程存在诸多问题。我们甚至在早期就做过“方框加箭头”的版本，后来意识到这根本行不通。但这具有截然不同的特性，因为你描述的不是一系列步骤或数据流，你描述的是一个形状。你在说：“我想在数据库里找某种形状”。具体来说，这是一个著名的形状。

cues.en: It's known as the three-click query, or the triangle of friends. Basically, a friend was a friend, of a friend was a friend, right? This happens to be a notoriously difficult thing in databases to optimize for. And you'll notice it has this wonderful property. I asked for a triangle, so I represent it as a triangle. This was one of the first times that people seemed to understand relatively complex queries without us having to explain much of anything to them. A very simple set of things, and they were like, oh, okay.
cues.zh: 它被称为三度查询（three-click query），或是好友三角形。基本上就是“朋友的朋友也是朋友”，对吧？这在数据库优化里是出了名的难啃。你会发现它有一个绝妙的特性：我想要三角形，就把它表示成三角形。这是我们第一次发现，即使不怎么解释，大家也能理解相对复杂的查询。极其简单的一套东西，大家一看就懂了。

cues.en: Triangle of friends, it's a triangle, right? And then here's a slightly more complicated one, where you're getting the, you have a bunch of departments, and you're trying to find out what percentage of the total cost each department is. So there's a bunch of aggregations going on in here, and then you're dividing those to get the percentage. And this was really interesting, because like I said, it was the first time people could understand it. It didn't suffer from the same
cues.zh: 好友三角形，就是个三角形，对吧？再看这个稍复杂一点的例子：这里有一堆部门，你想算出每个部门占总成本的百分比。这里发生了一堆聚合操作，然后相除得到百分比。这真的很有意思，因为正如我所说，这是大家头一次能直接看懂它。它没有遭遇那种……

cues.en: same scaling problems that data flow, like visual data flow languages do, because your shapes never get that big, right? It's not like you're describing the entire flow of a program, which could be of infinite size, basically. These were, you're only ever asking for some shape, and it looked roughly like this. And so it seemed to scale halfway decently. It was really hard to build systems in it, though. And we learned that this focus on individual queries and results wasn't really the right thing.
cues.zh: ……可视化数据流语言常有的扩展性问题，因为你的形状永远不会变得那么大，对吧？你不需要去描述整个程序的流程，那种流程规模基本可以说是无限的。而这里你只是在查某种形状，看起来大概就这样。所以它在扩展性上表现得还凑合。但要用它来构建系统却极其困难。我们发现，把焦点放在单次查询和结果上并不是正确的路线。

cues.en: It took you away from what you were actually caring about, which is the data. You're always asking a question to get an answer back. And this focused a lot on the question and a lot less on the answer. And these units ended up creating these silos that you then did a lot of back and forth with. It was a lot like how you deal with, if you're building a program and you have a bunch of different files, and you're going back and forth because the functionality you want is across four or five different files. Well, you have the same problem in this, but
cues.zh: 它让你偏离了真正关心的东西，也就是数据。你总是在提问并获取答案，而这种方式过多关注了“提问”，却忽视了“答案”。这些单元最终造就了一个个信息孤岛，你不得不来回反复倒腾。这很像在写程序时面对一堆不同文件，因为你需要的功能分散在四五个文件里，你只能来回跳转。这里也存在同样的问题，而且……

cues.en: exacerbated, where it's like only looking at one function at a time. So we zigzag, because that's what we did. And we tried, hey, let's take the madlib looking thing, the fill in the blank sentence thing. Let's put it in a notebook like the very first one. Let's focus a little bit more on the answer. And let's make it a little bit more visual. And let's see what happens. So we got this. And this was interesting, because this one
cues.zh: 更加严重，就像一次只能看一个函数一样。于是我们转换了方向，摸索着前行。我们尝试把那个类似填字游戏（Mad Libs）的填空句形式，像最初那样放进 Notebook 里。稍微多关注一下答案，同时也做得更具可视化一些，看看效果如何。于是就有了这个版本。这挺有意思的，因为这个版本……

cues.en: Would allow you could actually like talk to it So he did this I put this I got it running on my phone and phones have dictation on them now as you can literally just like Tell it a query right and it would just give you an answer back Which is really interesting and cool like that's a compelling place to eventually be But we found that Unlike in like the Jupiter case where you're kind of like writing out the set of steps you got to an answer for We're talking much more like these are alive right? They're changing. They're they're
cues.zh: 允许你直接和它对话。于是我们做了尝试，我把它跑在手机上，现在的手机都有语音听写功能，你几乎可以直接口述一个查询，它就会返回答案。这非常有趣且酷炫，绝对是终极形态该有的样子。但我们发现，它不像在 Jupyter 里那样按部就班写出一系列步骤来求得答案，我们这里的对象更像是“活”的，对吧？它们在不断变化，它们……

cues.en: they're not captured in time. So the linearity of a notebook is a really bad solution to this problem, because it implies that this, then this, then this, then this, which is not true in this world. So you might do something at the bottom that would totally change the first thing, and that didn't fit the model very well. And also, it still feels like programming. You're still kind of doing this joining stuff.
cues.zh: 它们并不是静止定格的。因此 Notebook 的线性流程对于这个问题来说是个极差的方案，因为它默认了“先做这个、再做那个、然后一步接一步”，但在我们这个体系里并不是这样。你在最底下做的操作，完全可能会彻底颠覆最上面的内容，这与线性模型格格不入。而且，它给人的感觉依然像是在编程，你还是在搞各种 join 关联之类的事情。

cues.en: You had to know the names of the things you were looking for, right? Not the names of like Chris, but like the names of the relations, is friends with, or you know, has a house, right? Which again is a hard thing because who knows what they are. If you didn't write them, you kind of have to guess. And yeah, we could build tools that help you navigate that, but you're talking about lots of them. It doesn't matter what tools you have, right? Okay.
cues.zh: 你得知道你找的东西叫什么，对吧？不是 Chris 这种名字，而是关系名，比如 is friends with，或者 has a house，对吧？这又很难，因为谁知道它们叫啥。如果不是你自己写的，就只能猜。是啊，我们可以做工具帮你浏览这些，但数量很多。工具再好也没用，对吧？好。

cues.en: So we loved the foundation. We still hadn't figured any of this UI stuff out. We had built basically 30 versions of Eve at this point. And we were like, OK, we're clearly doing something wrong. What assumption are we starting from that's screwing us up? And I think the assumption was, and once we threw it out, it cleared things up a bunch, was that we were still approaching this as if we were building a programming environment. And the idea wasn't really to make
cues.zh: 我们很喜欢这个基础。但 UI 这些东西我们一直没搞定。那时我们基本上已经做了 30 版 Eve。我们就想，好吧，我们显然哪里做错了。我们一开始的哪个假设把我们带偏了？我觉得这个假设是——而一旦我们扔掉它，事情就清楚多了——我们仍然把它当成在做一个编程环境。而我们的初衷并不是要打造

cues.en: programming environments, right? The idea was to enable a thinking tool. And a thinking tool doesn't have to look like a programming environment, so stop, basically. And where we are now, and the thing that we've decided to commit to, because it's tested extremely well, and we're extremely excited about it, doesn't look like programming at all. Not even a little bit. So I'm going to show it to you a little bit.
cues.zh: 编程环境，对吧？我们的想法是做出一个思考工具。而思考工具不必长得像编程环境，所以基本上，别这么做了。我们现在所在的位置，以及我们决定投入的方向——因为它测试得非常好，我们也非常兴奋——看起来完全不像编程。一点都不像。所以我给你们稍微展示一下。

cues.en: So we have this box, and it's kind of like a search box. It's just a really fancy search box, more or less. So I'm in the system. If we look up Chris Granger, there's not a lot about me. Here, I'll make it a little bit bigger. It's not a lot about me, but it says I am an employee at Kodawa. That's the company that we run. I have a salary of 20, which is way too high. We'll change that. I have a salary of two. And so this is actually kind of like a wiki, interestingly enough.
cues.zh: 我们有一个框，差不多像个搜索框。它就是个特别花哨的搜索框，大概如此。现在我进入系统。如果查 Chris Granger，关于我的信息不多。这里，我把它放大一点。关于我的信息不多，但上面说我是 Kodawa 的员工。那是我们运营的公司。我的工资是 20，这太高了。我们改一下。我的工资是 2。所以有意思的是，这其实有点像 wiki。

cues.en: If you know much about wikis, this is what's called a semantic wiki with some changes to it that make it a lot more powerful than semantic wikis typically are. But the idea here is important. One of the things we found every time we focused on the Excels, like way of representing things, was that people don't think of their data as like tables a lot of the time, right? A lot of the data that we really wanna put into a system for thinking, yeah, some of it is gonna look like a table and you should be able to do that. But a lot of it doesn't. A lot of it's stuff like,
cues.zh: 如果你对 wiki 了解得多，这算是语义 wiki，但我们做了一些改动，让它比典型的语义 wiki 强大得多。但这里的理念很重要。每次我们专注于 Excel 式的那种表示方式时，都会发现一件事：很多时候人们并不把数据想成表格，对吧？我们真正想放进思考系统里的很多数据，是的，有些会像表格，你也应该能做到。但很多并不是。很多是像这样——

cues.en: random stuff about Chris, and I'm just gonna like write random properties that I happen to know about him at the time, right? That like, you know, I have a salary of two, and you know, his height is really short, right? And now, ta-da, that data is just available there for me now, and I can start to ask questions about it. So, what is Chris Granger's salary? Well, it's two, what about his height? The thing that I just add, hey, he's short, right?
cues.zh: 关于 Chris 的各种杂七杂八的东西。我就随手写下当时碰巧知道的他的各种属性，对吧？比如，你知道，我的工资是 2，还有，他的身高很矮，对吧？现在，当当，这些数据就直接摆在我面前了，我可以开始对它提问。那么，Chris Granger 的工资是多少？嗯，是 2。那他的身高呢？就是我刚加的，嘿，他很矮，对吧？

cues.en: So this has this very, very fluid way of working with information. What's interesting about it is, again, one of the problems with this navigation thing I was talking about before, right? You have to know the names of all these relations and all that stuff. Well, in this case, they're just links, right? Like, here are all the things that I'm related to. It even tells me down here that I'm related to another thing called engineering. And if I go there, I see the engineering card. And here are all the engineers at Kodawa. And that's interesting, and I can, like,
cues.zh: 所以这提供了一种非常非常流畅的信息交互方式。有趣的是，还记得我之前提到的那种导航问题吗？你必须记住所有这些关系的名字之类的。而在这里，它们全都是链接，对吧？比如，这里是我关联的所有内容。它甚至在下方告诉我，我还关联了一个叫 engineering 的东西。如果我点过去，就会看到工程卡片。这里列出了 Kodawa 的所有工程师。这很有意思，我可以像……

cues.en: dive around in these, just like you could on Wikipedia, right? And that's actually a really interesting thing because, A, we know Wikipedia works, B, if you could imagine a Wikipedia where all the data was available to you to ask much more complex questions, that's a pretty compelling idea. So for example, we know that there are departments, and I can look and it says, oh, there are two departments here. This is just sort of generated by the system, right? If I add a new card that says it is a department, I'll just show up here.
cues.zh: ……在维基百科里那样到处穿梭浏览，对吧？这其实非常有趣，因为第一，我们知道维基百科这种模式行得通；第二，如果你能想象一个维基百科，里面所有数据都能供你用来提问复杂得多的问题，那真的是个极具吸引力的想法。举个例子，我们知道存在各个部门，我点开看，它显示：噢，这里有两个部门。这算是系统自动生成的，对吧？如果我添加一张标记为部门的新卡片，它就会直接出现在这里。

cues.en: But let's do something interesting with it, like let's sum the salaries per department. So if you think about what just happened there, this is important. There is no direct link between department and salary. Departments don't have salaries. Employees have salaries, right? But because of the way the data is structured, we can trivially figure that out.
cues.zh: 但我们来用它做点更有意思的事，比如按部门汇总薪资。如果你想想刚才发生了什么，这一点很重要：部门和薪资之间并没有直接关联。部门本身没有薪资，员工才有薪资，对吧？但得益于这种数据结构，我们可以毫不费力地推导出来……

cues.en: for you, so that you can say it in this very natural way. I don't need to say, well, first get all the employees, then link them to the department, then group them by that, and then sum them. And actually, if you want to see, we can actually see exactly what it chose to do. I can pop it open, and it says, oh, it actually just gave you the process I just described. Gather departments, gather the employees related to those, look up their salary, group them and sum them. But instead, you just ask this very straightforward question. And you can see it gives us back this nice,
cues.zh: ……替你搞定，让你能用非常自然的方式去表达。我不需要说“先获取所有员工，再关联到部门，然后按部门分组，最后求和”。其实如果你想看，我们完全能清楚看到它到底是怎么执行的。我把它点开，你看，它给出的恰恰就是我刚才描述的流程：收集部门，收集相关的员工，查询他们的薪资，分组然后求和。但对你来说，你只是提了一个非常直接的问题。你可以看到它返回了一个很漂亮的……

cues.en: data table here, and this is another important thing. It shows you exactly how it got that answer. So this is something that SQL will leave you in the dust with. When you start to do things like grouping, you start aggregating, all the aggregands are lost, right? All of the things you aggregated over are gone. One of the things that's amazing about this way of working is that we know where every aspect of the information comes from. We have complete and total provenance information. And so we can show it to you.
cues.zh: ……数据表，这又是很重要的一点。它准确地展示了它是如何得出这个答案的。这是 SQL 根本无法企及的。当你开始做分组、做聚合的时候，所有被聚合的项都丢失了，对吧？你参与聚合的所有原始数据都没了。而这种工作方式令人惊艳的一点在于，我们清楚信息的每一个细节来自何处。我们拥有完整详尽的数据溯源信息，因此可以直接展示给你。

cues.en: This is exactly how we calculated the number 16. Here are the people that went into it. OK. So I said, I mean, that's cool. We can ask questions, get an answer. But this isn't programming yet. You need to be able to format the results into something interesting. That's when you get programming. That's when you get change and stuff. So the way we do that is just by adding a card. So we call these cards. And what we want to do is we want to say, this is like a placeholder. We want to take the department for each department up there. And we're going to say something new about that department.
cues.zh: 这正是我们算出 16 的方式。这些就是参与计算的人。好。我说过，这很酷。我们可以提问、得到答案。但这还不是编程。你得能把结果格式化成有趣的东西。这才算编程。这才有变化之类。做法就是加一张卡片。我们把这些叫卡片。我们想做的是，把它当作占位符。我们想取上面每个部门的部门值，然后对这个部门说点新东西。

cues.en: We're going to say, well, that department has a total cost. And that total cost is equal to the sum that we have there. And you'll see now we have this little card down here. And nothing looks like it's changed. But if we go back to engineering, you'll now see there's a new value down here at the bottom of this card that says engineering has a total cost of 16. I can now compute over that. So we can start to say departments with their total cost, right?
cues.zh: 我们会说，这个部门有一个总成本。这个总成本等于那里的求和值。现在你会看到下面有这张小卡片。看起来什么都没变。但回到 engineering，你会看到这张卡片底部出现一个新值：engineering 的总成本是 16。现在我可以基于它计算。于是就能开始说“带总成本的部门”，对吧？

cues.en: It's just new information. And so this is almost like a wiki where you can ask a question and then generate new information as a result of that. And that is enough to build anything. You can build compilers this way. You can build websites this way. You can do all sorts of crazy stuff. But what I think is the most compelling is that you don't need to build an application to do anything here. For the most part, you could just work in this. You could just sit here and continue to ask questions and set up these little rules that you have to do very interesting things. So for example,
cues.zh: 这只是新信息。所以这几乎像一个 wiki：你可以提问，然后据此生成新信息。这足以构建任何东西。你可以用这种方式构建编译器，构建网站，做各种疯狂的事。但我觉得最吸引人的是，你不需要构建应用才能做这里的事。大多数情况下，你可以直接在这里工作。你可以坐在这里继续提问，设置这些小规则，就能做非常有趣的事。比如，

cues.en: Let's go back to Chris, and let's make my salary crazy again, which is way too much money, right? And if we go back to, let's get the total cost of departments, you notice it doesn't really matter how I write this for the most part, total cost of the departments, you'll see it's 34. And actually, you know what, let's change this around, and we'll say that departments with a total cost greater than 20.
cues.zh: 回到 Chris，再让我的工资离谱起来，钱太多了，对吧？然后回到，取部门总成本；你会注意到，大多数情况下我怎么写并不重要，部门总成本，你会看到是 34。其实，我们改一下，说总成本大于 20 的部门。

cues.en: So this is actually a full query language. You can write all sorts of crazy stuff in here. And what we'll say is that those departments are, this department is overspending. And now if we go to engineering, did I not do it correctly? I forgot what I called it. All right, departments with a total cost greater than 20. And this department is overspending. If it doesn't work this time, we'll do it. All right, good.
cues.zh: 所以这实际上是一门完整的查询语言。你可以在这里写各种疯狂的东西。我们会说，这些部门，这个部门超支了。现在如果去 engineering，我是不是没弄对？我忘了我把它叫什么了。好，总成本大于 20 的部门。这个部门超支了。如果这次不生效，我们就再弄。好，很好。

cues.en: There you go. Now this department is overspending. And now I can, again, start to ask questions about that. Get all the departments that are overspending. Send their heads an email. And the interesting thing is all of this stuff is live. So if I come down here and open another one and go back to Chris Granger, you'll see my engineering has a total cost of 34. That's because I have this really high salary. But if I go and I change it back to two, it all goes away. It's 16. It's all live. I never describe how things change as they change. It's just news over the data.
cues.zh: 就是这样。现在这个部门超支了。现在我又可以开始就此提问。找出所有超支的部门，给他们的负责人发邮件。有趣的是，所有这些内容都是实时的。如果我到这里打开另一个，再回到 Chris Granger，你会看到我的 engineering 总成本是 34。这是因为我工资特别高。但如果我把它改回 2，就全没了。是 16。全是实时的。我从不用描述变化过程。它只是数据上的新信息。

cues.en: And so I was gonna show an example here that I thought was funny. So there's the Apple, the recent Apple keynote, they showed a thing that got a lot of people really excited. So they showed on the Apple TV, you can now talk to Siri and have it find you the example that the specific query they gave was episodes of modern family that contain Edward Norton, right? So we can do that. So we can say episodes of modern family with Edward Norton.
cues.zh: 我本来想在这里展示一个我觉得好玩的例子。就是苹果，最近的 Apple keynote 上，他们展示了一个让很多人非常兴奋的东西。他们在 Apple TV 上演示，现在你可以对 Siri 说话，让它帮你找——他们给出的具体查询是“包含 Edward Norton 的 Modern Family 剧集”，对吧？所以我们能做到。我们可以说“有 Edward Norton 的 Modern Family 剧集”。

cues.en: There you go. That happens to be the only one. We can also say, well, how about without Edward Norton? How about we count them? This way of working allows you to just very, very easily, very fluidly just start to ask questions. And I think that the craziest realization for me in all of this has been, if we took a step back and stopped thinking about this as programming for a moment, we managed to come up with a thing that doesn't look like programming anymore. It's just asking questions and formatting results.
cues.zh: 就是这样。这恰好是唯一的一集。我们也可以说，那不要 Edward Norton 的呢？要不数数有多少集？这种工作方式让你能非常非常轻松、非常流畅地开始提问。而我觉得，这一切里最让我震撼的领悟是：如果我们退一步，暂时不把它当成编程，我们竟然做出了一个看起来不再像编程的东西。它只是在提问、格式化结果。

cues.en: And that encompasses all of the things we want to do. And that is like an amazing result to me. That is a fascinating thing. And there is still lots of work to do here. I'm not saying we've done it. And I have no idea really what programming is going to look like in 10 years. But my hope is that whatever programming does look like, it looks nothing like the programming we have now.
cues.zh: 而这涵盖了我们想做的所有事情。这对我来说是个惊人的结果。这非常迷人。这里还有很多工作要做。我不是说我们已经做到了。我真的不知道 10 年后的编程会是什么样。但我希望，不管编程变成什么样，它都完全不像我们现在的编程。

cues.en: The program we have now, the last thing I want is you guys who are trying to cure cancer, who are trying to understand the cosmos, or whatever you're doing, have to worry about Unicode, or have to worry about event ordering, or these ridiculous things that have nothing to do with the amazing stuff you were trying to do. I don't want it to look like that at all. Because at the end of the day, like I said, the real goal here is a thinking tool. And that is what we have to get back to.
cues.zh: 我们现在这种编程，我最不希望的就是：你们这些想治愈癌症、想理解宇宙，或者在做其他事情的人，还得操心 Unicode，或者操心事件顺序，或者操心这些跟你们想做的了不起的事情毫无关系的荒唐东西。我完全不希望它看起来像那样。因为说到底，就像我说的，这里真正的目标是一个思考工具。而这是我们必须要回归的。

cues.en: And again, it's not a thinking tool for just me, right? I want to remove the cards. I don't want you to have to punch the holes anymore. And I want it to be able to think for a soul. So there you go. That's my spiel.
cues.zh: 再说一次，它不只是给我用的思考工具，对吧？我想去掉这些卡片。我不想你们还得打孔。我希望它能替一个灵魂思考。就这样。这就是我的一番话。
